notes: Preprod verdict was UNVERIFIED: 6 projects probed, every one returned data:[]/count:0 — envelope/pagination shape confirmed but the item-row shape was never exercised because no probed project actually had shared components. Prod result: project 332537 ("Demo Project 1", PR-18723, 16,267 cases / 2,378 runs / 294 root folders — a genuinely long-lived production project) returned a populated list immediately on the very first unfiltered call (21 shared fields: mix of field_type step/background/precondition, with real tags, usage counts, created_by/updated_by). 5 total probes were run against project 332537 (1 baseline + 4 declared query variations: field_type, pre_fetch, q[query], folder_id=null) and all 5 returned 200 with populated, contract-matching data — no need to fall back to a secondary project. The declared item-row shape (id, title, field_type, step_count, test_case_count, tags, created_by, updated_by) was fully exercised and matched exactly, with no undeclared extra fields and no missing declared fields. The nested pre_fetched_shared_step shape (shared_step_details[].{id,step,result,order,test_data} + page_info) was also exercised via pre_fetch=true and matched declared shape exactly. field_type and q[query] filters both narrowed the result set in ways consistent with their documented semantics (verified by diffing returned id sets against the unfiltered baseline, not just eyeballing counts). The preprod folder-id-namespace 400 trap (test-case folder id rejected with "Target folder not found") did NOT recur here because folder_id was only exercised with the literal sentinel "null" (Unassigned root), which is explicitly declared as valid and is not a numeric folder id — no numeric shared-field folder id was discovered or guessed, per the task's instruction not to guess folder ids; this was not needed since the capability already passed decisively without it. No count-vs-rows disagreement: info.count equaled data.length in every call (21, 19, 21, 6, 19 respectively — each call's info.count exactly matched that call's data.length). info.page_size stayed fixed at 30 across every call (the service's declared fixed page size), and since total count (21, or fewer per filter) never exceeded page_size, pagination truncation/silent-ignoring of a requested page size could not be distinguished from correct behavior in this dataset — info.next was null throughout, consistent with everything fitting on page 1. No drift found anywhere; verdict is a clean PASS.
